title: PC1 explains 99% of the engagement variance — score users on it?

scenario.role: You're the lifecycle/growth analyst at Fernglow
scenario.situation: Nadia, the growth lead, ran PCA over four engagement metrics — page_views, purchase_count, email_opens, days_since_signup — to build a single "engagement score." PC1 explains 99% of the variance, and she wants to rank every user by it, targeting the bottom of the ranking with a win-back campaign next week.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "PC1 captures 99% of the variance across our four engagement metrics — it's basically our engagement score already built. Let's rank users on it and win back the bottom tier."
scenario.question: Does PC1 actually identify the users at risk of not coming back — the ones a win-back campaign should target? Check what PC1 is really measuring, and how well it (or any of the four raw metrics) predicts 90-day retention, before targeting goes out on it.

columns.name: days_since_signup
columns.description: Days since the user signed up (1-365)

columns.name: page_views
columns.description: Total page views in the last 90 days

columns.name: purchase_count
columns.description: Purchases/subscriptions completed in the last 90 days (0-10)

columns.name: email_opens
columns.description: Marketing emails opened in the last 90 days (0-20)

columns.name: retained_90d
columns.description: 1 if the user was still active 90 days later — the outcome a win-back campaign should be targeting

columns.name: pc1_score
columns.description: The user's score on the first principal component, computed from PCA fit on the four raw (unscaled) metrics above

guidingQuestions: Correlate pc1_score with page_views, purchase_count, email_opens, and days_since_signup individually. Which raw column does PC1 actually track?
Correlate pc1_score with retained_90d. Is that relationship strong enough to target a win-back campaign on?
Now correlate each of the four raw metrics with retained_90d individually. Which one is the real predictor?
Compare the ranges of the four columns. Which one has, by far, the biggest scale — and what does that do to a PCA fit on unscaled features?
If Nadia targets the bottom of the PC1 ranking for win-back, what kind of user will actually get targeted — and who gets missed?
suggestedApproach: Correlate pc1_score against each of the four raw inputs to see which one it's really summarizing.
Correlate pc1_score against retained_90d directly — that's the number that matters for targeting, not the explained-variance figure.
Correlate each raw metric against retained_90d separately, and compare those correlations to PC1's.
Check the scale of each input column — page_views should dwarf the other three, explaining why PCA loaded almost entirely onto it.
Conclude which metric should actually drive the win-back targeting, and why 'explains the most variance' isn't the same question as 'predicts who comes back.'

notebook.intro: Five steps: find out what PC1 is really summarising, then check whether it predicts the thing you care about.

cells.title: Find out what PC1 is made of
cells.explain: Correlate pc1_score against each raw input to see which one it is really tracking.
cells.code:
inputs = ["days_since_signup", "page_views", "purchase_count", "email_opens"]
loadings = df[inputs].corrwith(df["pc1_score"]).sort_values(ascending=False)
print("correlation of PC1 with each input:")
loadings.round(3)
cells.reads: PC1 is almost entirely one input. It is not a blend of engagement; it is a rename.

cells.title: Check PC1 against the outcome
cells.explain: The number that matters for targeting is how well PC1 predicts retention, not how much variance it explains.
cells.code:
pc1_corr = df["pc1_score"].corr(df["retained_90d"])
print(f"correlation of PC1 with retained_90d: {pc1_corr:.3f}")
df.groupby(pd.qcut(df["pc1_score"], 5, labels=False, duplicates="drop"))["retained_90d"].mean().round(3) * 100
cells.reads: For all its explained variance, PC1 barely moves retention across its range.

cells.title: Check each raw metric against the outcome
cells.explain: Correlate every input with retention separately and compare them to PC1.
cells.code:
raw_corr = df[inputs].corrwith(df["retained_90d"]).sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False)
print("correlation with retained_90d:")
raw_corr.round(3)
cells.reads: At least one raw metric predicts retention far better than PC1 does.

cells.title: Check the scales
cells.explain: PCA is scale-sensitive. Look at the spread of each input in raw units.
cells.reads: One column's scale dwarfs the others, which is exactly why PCA loaded onto it and ignored the rest.

cells.title: Explained variance is not relevance
cells.explain: Put PC1's correlation with the outcome beside the best raw metric's.
cells.code:
best = raw_corr.abs().idxmax()
pd.DataFrame(
    {"correlation with retention": [pc1_corr, df[best].corr(df["retained_90d"])]},
    index=["PC1 (explains the most variance)", best + " (predicts the outcome)"],
).round(3)
cells.reads: Explaining the most variance answers a question nobody asked. Targeting should follow the metric that predicts who comes back.

teachingNote.naiveRead: PC1 explains 99% of the variance across the four engagement metrics. That reads like PC1 has distilled almost everything worth knowing about a user into one number — ready to rank and target on.
teachingNote.theTrap: PCA finds the direction of maximum *variance*, with no idea which column predicts the outcome you actually care about. page_views ranges into the thousands while purchase_count tops out at 10 and email_opens at 20 — page_views' raw variance is so much larger that PC1 loads almost entirely onto it (loading ≈ 1.00 on page_views, ≈ 0 on everything else). PC1 isn't an engagement score; it's page_views wearing a disguise. And page_views barely relates to 90-day retention (correlation ≈ -0.01) — retention is actually driven by purchase_count (correlation ≈ 0.38, by far the strongest signal), with email_opens a weak secondary factor (≈ 0.06). The metric that 'explains the most variance' is nearly useless for predicting who comes back.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Don't target the win-back campaign off PC1. Correlate each raw metric against retained_90d directly: purchase_count is the strongest single predictor (≈ 0.38 — more purchases, much higher retention), email_opens is a weak secondary signal (≈ 0.06), and both page_views and PC1 are essentially uncorrelated with retention (≈ -0.01 either way). If Nadia wants a defensible target list, rank by purchase_count directly (or standardize all four metrics before running PCA, so page_views can't dominate) — not by an unscaled PC1 that's quietly just re-reporting page views. As built, targeting the bottom of the PC1 ranking would pull in low-page-view users regardless of whether they've actually purchased, while missing plenty of low-purchase users who browse a lot and still won't come back.
howToGetThere: Fit PCA on the four raw (unscaled) metrics; check explained_variance_ratio_ — PC1 alone captures ≈ 99%.
Inspect PC1's loadings: page_views ≈ 1.00, the other three ≈ 0 — PC1 is essentially page_views restated.
Correlate pc1_score with retained_90d directly: ≈ -0.01 — no real relationship, despite the huge variance share.
Correlate each raw metric with retained_90d: purchase_count ≈ 0.38 (strongest), email_opens ≈ 0.06, page_views ≈ -0.01.
Compare column scales: page_views ranges into the thousands vs. single digits/tens for the others — explaining why unscaled PCA collapsed onto it.
teachingNote.lesson: Explained variance measures how much a component captures about the *spread* of your inputs, not whether it relates to the outcome you actually care about — and PCA is scale-sensitive, so an unscaled feature with a big numeric range will dominate the first component regardless of its real-world importance. Before ranking or targeting users on a component, correlate it against the actual outcome, and check whether one raw input's scale is doing all the work. A score that summarizes 99% of the data's variance can still summarize none of what you need to know.
